opening.headline: Explore how data protection requirements and platform constraints limit the promotion process, and evaluate the design of promotion and permission changes.
body: The validated model is waiting for promotion, while the training data is still protected by masking policies and operational permissions have not been properly revoked. Changing permissions all at once could result in exposure or outages during the transition state.

In this lesson, we distinguish the protection requirements for data that models access, examine promotion checklists and the order of permission modifications, compare permission-level differences across platforms, and evaluate whether designs are appropriate in two case studies.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The promotion-eligible model can distinguish the protection conditions of the accessed data.
Can assess the suitability of promotion and permission change designs

screens.title: Protection requirements and platform constraints hinder promotion.
screens.lead: Let's examine issues discovered just before promotion. While reading the scene, consider what else besides model performance should be verified.

paragraphs: The validated model is awaiting promotion. The performance metrics are sufficient, and promotion appears to be merely a matter of updating one alias. However, the data used for training this model is subject to a masking policy.

When upgraded, the access permissions of users and services in the operating environment to this model and data have not yet been fully defined. During training, we observed masked values, but in operations, we might need to access the original data, or conversely, operational accounts might not have access to the required data.
In addition, the way and order in which permissions are granted vary across platforms. If permissions are changed all at once, it may result in exposure or outages during intermediate states.

In this course, we examine how promotion candidate models distinguish the protection conditions of the data they access, and evaluate whether the promotion and permission modification designs are appropriate.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If the model's performance is sufficient, is upgrade preparation complete? While conducting the class, directly list the items to verify before upgrading.

visual.alt: The promotion arrow is blocked by masking policy, operational permissions, and platform restriction cards.

screens.outro: First, let us recall our organization's promotion review process.

screens.title: Do you check data permissions at the time of promotion?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process is displayed. Please first think about the answer on your own before clicking it.

items.prompt: Is there a data access item in the current promotion checklist besides the model performance item?
items.answer: Performance metrics are often available without data access provisions. Since a model operates by reading data, data protection conditions must be included in promotion criteria. The checklist from this course serves as the starting point.

items.prompt: What happens when the operational service account reads data with different permissions than during learning?
items.answer: The same query can yield different results depending on the account. Columns with masking return different values during training compared to inference, leading to a different input distribution for the model and potentially altering prediction quality. Conversely, accessing the original data introduces exposure risks.

items.prompt: Where are records of permission changes kept?
items.answer: If you don't know the record location, it's difficult to respond to the request. It's necessary to record the timestamp, actor, and reason of the permission change together with the escalation record. Then, we examine which items to retain in the following screen.

screens.outro: Based on the questions that come to mind, let's first distinguish the protection conditions.

screens.title: Distinguish protection conditions: data accessed by the model
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the protection conditions and inspection questions to verify before promotion.

tabs.label: Lineage
tabs.body: The starting point is verifying, via lineage, the tables and columns that a promotion-eligible model reads during learning and inference. Lineage shows where sensitive data originates and where it is consumed downstream, thus serving as a basis for compliance audits. The audit question is this: Which columns does this model read that are subject to protection conditions? If there is no input column list, all subsequent audits become speculative, making lineage the first and most critical step.

tabs.label: row filter
tabs.body: Row filtering limits which rows can be viewed. It is essential to verify that the rows used for training are the same as those accessible during operations. Since query results may vary depending on the user at query time, it is certain to directly inspect the data from the operational perspective. The key question to assess is whether the operational account sees the same rows as during training. If the row scope differs, the model may process data from groups it was not trained on.

tabs.label: column mask
tabs.body: Column mask determines how values appear. If the access subject differs between training and operational phases, the same query might receive masked values, leading to different inputs. The extent of impact varies depending on the masking method, such as hashing or partial obfuscation. A key question to verify is whether the values received during operational service match the form of values observed during training.

tabs.label: ABAC tag
tabs.body: A column that consistently applies policies using tag-based ABAC must verify whether tags are retained prior to promotion. If tags are lost, the policy no longer applies and protection is removed. Tags may not automatically carry over to newly created tables or copies, so verification is necessary. The inspection must check not only tag names but also whether the policy is actually being applied. The inspection question is whether the required tags are properly attached to the columns that the model reads.

screens.outro: Since we've distinguished the protection conditions, we'll now review the checklist to be used before promotion and the order for permission changes.

screens.title: Promotion checklist example and permission change sequence
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to review each checklist item and task sequence one by one.

steps.title: Checklist 1: Lineage
steps.body: The model verifies the lineage of tables and columns it reads. Without knowing which columns are being input, it's impossible to determine which protection conditions need to be checked. To avoid missing the flow of sensitive data, the model must examine not only the tables it directly reads but also the upstream sources.

steps.title: Checklist 2: Masking Results of the Operational Entity
steps.body: Verify that the data permissions of the operating entity, such as a service account or role, match the masking results observed during training. Compare the actual query results obtained when operating as the entity against the values observed during training. If the values differ, hold off on promotion and investigate the cause. It is also advisable to record the comparison results.

steps.title: Checklist 3: Model Usage Permissions
steps.body: Grant model access only to the principals that need it. Use model permissions in Unity Catalog; in Snowflake, distinguish `USAGE` from `READ` according to the inference method. Give narrower permissions to callers who do not need to inspect model internals. Starting with narrow access and expanding it when needed is safer than granting broad access and reducing it later.

steps.title: Work sequence
steps.body: First, prepare model permissions and data permissions, then promote the alias. Reversing the order would result in aliases pointing to the new version while lacking permissions, causing failures, or creating overly permissive sections that lead to exposure.

steps.title: Thank you record
steps.body: We record the timing, actor, and reason for permission changes and promotions in audit logs. When issues arise, these logs allow us to trace which change was the cause and provide explanations during audits. Records stored in a system format are more reliable than those relying on human memory.

screens.outro: The procedure has been verified; now I'll compare the constraints that vary by platform.

screens.title: Platform constraints and audit logs
screens.lead: Read the table and compare how authorization and change ownership differ between Databricks and Snowflake.

data.notes: If the platform differs, the same promotion may involve different permission levels. Therefore, design documentation must specify exactly which objects are granted what permissions. Permission changes are logged in audit records alongside promotions. Since the entity that can modify permissions is restricted across all platforms, it's essential to verify in advance whether the promotion administrator can directly modify permissions. It's a common cause of delays when an administrator without proper permissions searches for a manager on the day of promotion. Document clearly in the promotion process who is responsible for changing which permissions. Remember that while the promotion itself is the same, in Databricks permissions are checked along the object hierarchy, whereas in Snowflake they are checked based on account privileges and roles.

screens.outro: Having confirmed the differences between the two platforms, let's apply the trained model, which was learned using masked data, to a sample case.

screens.title: Explanation Example: Upgrade Conditions of a Model Trained with Masked Data
screens.lead: This lesson explains the process of upgrading a model trained on masked customer data. Select the right arrow to proceed step by step.

steps.title: Case conditions
steps.body: We intend to deploy a churn prediction model trained on a masked customer table within an email column into production. Performance validation has been completed, and now we are at the stage of verifying data protection requirements prior to promotion.

steps.title: Step 1: Verify the values during learning
steps.body: During learning, verify whether the model pipeline saw masked values or original values. The clue lies in which group the account that executed the learning pipeline belongs to. If learning was performed using a developer's personal account, you might have seen different values compared to a general service account.

steps.title: Step 2: Verify Operational Role
steps.body: Verify that the operational service role is applying the same mask. If reading the original, the learning distribution differs and exposure risks are present. In this case, the greatest risk is precisely this inconsistency. A model trained on masked values will produce different predictions when given original email inputs, and at the same time, the original input might be logged in service logs.

steps.title: Step 3: Advance after correct selection
steps.body: Align the mask and tag first, grant the model usage permissions, then move the alias. By following this order, the protection conditions are maintained even when the alias is moved. Conversely, if the alias is moved first, the original resource could briefly flow into service.

steps.title: Step 4: Record
steps.body: Records both promotion history and permission changes. When retraining or rolling back with the same model later, you can verify the conditions under which promotion occurred.

steps.title: organizing
steps.body: The promotion criteria for this case are three: first, the masking result of the operating entity must be identical to that during training; second, the model access permissions must be granted only to entities that require them; third, the permission preparation must occur before the alias migration. If any of these conditions are not met, promotion is deferred. Deferral is not a failure but a safe judgment to allow for further review and re-evaluation once the conditions are satisfied.

screens.outro: We have analyzed the case; now let's evaluate the suitability of the two design options.

screens.title: Explanation: Assessment of Suitability for Promotion and Authority Change Design
screens.lead: Compare design options A and B in the table to see whether they meet the four evaluation criteria. The instructor's judgment is provided in the description below the table.

data.caption: Comparison of Design Options A and B by Criterion
columns: Design Option A: Change once, just before promotion
Design Option B: Separate into verification, preparation, movement, and recording phases
rows: Protection condition satisfied
There is no step to verify masking alignment during learning and during operation, thus satisfaction cannot be guaranteed.
Start with verifying Lineage and protection conditions to confirm compliance. If a discrepancy is found, proceed to the next step. The verification result becomes the input for the next step.
Exposure of intermediate states
Model permissions, data permissions, and alias can change simultaneously, potentially leading to exposure or outage periods during the change.
Prepare permissions first and move the alias to the end to reduce intermediate exposure.
Undo possibility
Multiple changes are mixed together, making it unclear which one to revert.

Alias movement can be easily reverted, and permission changes are separately tracked in logs. Issues can be isolated and examined in isolation. Especially when permissions are already pre-configured, alias movement becomes a brief operation, making reversion immediate.
Record keeping
Combined in a single operation, changes cannot be easily distinguished by their timestamps and performers.
Record progress at each step and finalize with a thank-you record.
data.notes: Design B satisfies all four criteria. Design A falls short in terms of intermediate states and audit trails. While Design A's speed is an advantage, in scenarios involving interdependent changes, speed is less safe than staged separation. Moreover, when issues arise in Design A, it becomes difficult to determine which specific change caused the problem, making recovery time considerably longer. Teams that frequently promote changes benefit more by breaking down processes into procedures as Design B does, making them repeatable. When making judgments, verify the four criteria in sequence. If any one criterion is not met, the design must be improved. This evaluation applies regardless of the platform, and a design passes review only if the weakness of any criterion can be clearly explained in words.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Summarizes the core of the lesson in one go.

paragraphs: Promotion involves not just moving a model, but also verifying both model and data permissions together. Before promotion, check the lineage, masking match, model usage permissions, permission change sequence, and audit records.

The key issue is whether data protection requirements are consistent during learning and during operations. First, prepare the permissions, then migrate the aliases, and finally document the changes. Since permission units and change agents vary by platform, specify them explicitly on a per-object basis in the design documentation.

Answering the initial question does not mean that promotion readiness is complete. You must also verify the protection conditions and permission hierarchy before promotion readiness is considered complete.

In practice, it would be helpful to compile this information into a single promotion checklist. The items should be organized in the following order: lineage verification, comparison of masking results from the operating entity, granting of model usage permissions, permission modifications, alias migration, and audit log sequence. By using the same checklist each time a new model is promoted, the variation in inspection levels across individuals can be reduced.

glossary.def: Conditions that restrict access, such as row filter, column mask, and ABAC tag policies, applied to the data.
Checklist to verify alignment between data protection requirements and permissions prior to model promotion.
This is an operation sequence that first prepares permissions and then performs alias migration later, thereby preventing intermediate exposure.
Records of authority changes and promotions, including the timestamp, performer, and reason.

misconceptions.myth: If the model performance is good, promotion is possible.
misconceptions.fact: You should verify that the data protection requirements are the same for both learning and operations.

misconceptions.myth: Permissions can be set after promotion.
misconceptions.fact: If the order is incorrect, exposure or failures may occur in an intermediate state, so permissions must be prepared first.

misconceptions.myth: The platform may differ, but the promotion procedure is the same.
misconceptions.fact: Permissions at the unit level and the entity performing the change must be specified separately in the design document for each object.

closing.lead: We will summarize the key points of today's class.
points: Promotion involves reviewing both the model and data permissions together.
Before promotion, check lineage, masking match, and model permissions.
Prepare the permissions first, move the alias, and then record the action.
Reflects platform-specific differences in authorization units into the design.
closing.reflectionLead: The following question is for your own reflection. Answers will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Is there a data permission and protection condition item in our promotion checklist?

title: Data protection requirements and promotion design

checks.q: Let's consider the model upgrade process in a safe sequence.
items: The model verifies the lineage and protection conditions of the tables and columns it reads.
Prepares the data permissions and model usage permissions for the operating entity.
Moves an alias up in hierarchy
Records the execution agent in audit logs when permissions are changed or upgraded.
checks.explain: Prepare permissions and protection conditions first, then move the alias to avoid exposure of intermediate states, and finally record the outcome.
checks.intro: We just learned the sequence for the upgrade process. Arrange it in a safe order. An unrecorded self-check.
checks.correctFeedback: The order is correct: confirmation, permission preparation, alias migration, then logging.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The order is incorrect. Alias movement must occur after permissions are prepared, and logging follows thereafter.

checks.q: When a model trained with masked email data is deployed, the operational service ends up reading the original, unmasked emails. What is the biggest issue here?
options: The original is more accurate, so model performance always improves.
At the moment of moving an alias, the mask policy is permanently deleted.
Learning and input distributions differ, leading to original exposure risks.
When Lineage breaks, the model version disappears.
checks.explain: If the operational role reads the original, it diverges from the learning distribution and introduces exposure risks. Masking and tagging must be applied first, followed by granting permissions and moving the alias.

wrong.0: Predictions may become misaligned when learning and input differ.
wrong.1: Promotion does not remove the mask policy.
wrong.3: Lineage and model versions are not eliminated under this situation.

checks.intro: Assess the operational risk of a model trained on masked data. This is an unrecorded self-audit.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. The change in input distribution and the original exposure are the biggest issues.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Think again. What happens when the values observed during learning differ from those read during operation?

checks.q: Why is Design Option A (changing model permissions, data permissions, and alias at once just before promotion) weaker than Design Option B (verification, permission preparation, alias migration, separation of records)?
options: Intermediate states are likely to be exposed and it is difficult to maintain change records.
because we are not using aliases
Because permissions are not granted at all
This is because Snowflake prohibits changing it all at once.
checks.explain: Changing all at once may result in exposure or outages during the transition and provides limited staging records. By breaking changes into stages, you can manage protection conditions, rollbacks, and maintain proper records.

wrong.1: Move the alias for both ends.
wrong.2: Change the permissions on both sides. The difference is only in order and separation.
wrong.3: A particular platform is not banned; rather, it is inherently weak by design standards.

checks.intro: Compare the two designs and identify their weaknesses. An unrecorded self-assessment.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. If you change it all at once, it may result in exposure of intermediate states and recording issues.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The reason is not a weakness in design A. Consider what happens when changes are made all at once—what section would be generated in that case.
